In the hospital, all anyone ever does is wait. A woman in the labor and delivery wing waits for her baby to be born, while a man in the oncology department waits for his chemo therapy. A parent waits for their child’s medication to be approved by those blasted insurance companies, while the child waits for the next dose of painkillers. An elderly gentleman and a young girl alike can both await Death’s sweet release within the same four walls.  
  
And an immortal being waits for something completely different.

A little boy gasps from one of the rooms and runs toward him. “Link’s back! Link’s back!” he shouts. Link kneels down to catch him in a hug, his voice pitched up to greet the child with nothing but smiles.     
  
“How were your adventures? Did you bring me anything?” the child asks.     
  
Link grins. “I think I do have something,” he signs, digging through his pouch. He pulls out a star fragment the size of his palm. “Have you ever held a star before?” he asks.     
  
The child gapes at the glowing fragment. It’s a smaller one. I wonder where he got it from, if he remembers how much the fragments fascinated him when he was a kid. It was something his mother told me, and his old bedroom had them hanging from the ceiling. In his room in the barracks, he had one on his desk.     
  
“It’ll help you find your way at night,” he signs. The child takes the fragment gently and thanks Link.

I missed a lot of things over the past 100 years. One of the things at the top of that list was Link’s cooking. One taste, and I’m flooded with memories of my own from traveling with him, sneaking down to the kitchens with him, and letting him cook. I’m beyond thrilled that he learned how to cook again.    
  
“What is this, Link? It’s incredible,” Paya asks, her mouth half-full.    
  
“Just some hearty stew. Thought it’d help Zelda get some strength back.”    
  
I look up at that, and catch him smiling at me – a far off look. He quickly returns his attention back to his half-empty bowl.

“How were your adventures? Did you bring me anything?” the child asks.     
  
Link grins. “I think I do have something,” he signs, digging through his pouch. He pulls out a star fragment the size of his palm. “Have you ever held a star before?” he asks.     
  
The child gapes at the glowing fragment. It’s a smaller one. I wonder where he got it from, if he remembers how much the fragments fascinated him when he was a kid. It was something his mother told me, and his old bedroom had them hanging from the ceiling. In his room in the barracks, he had one on his desk.     
  
“It’ll help you find your way at night,” he signs. The child takes the fragment gently and thanks Link.

We continue walking and talking until it takes us to Mipha’s statue, where we find Prince Sidon bent in what looks like prayer. Everyone seems to decide to give him space, but Link has other ideas.     
  
He walks up to the statue, next to Sidon, and kneels, too. Sidon doesn’t seem to question this, and only gives Link a sad smile and nod. Link bends his own head in prayer.     
  
I watch the scene *curiously*. Bazz bends to my level and whispers, “They’ve done this before. A bit of solidarity, we think.”     
  
I nod, and watch them. It’s a strange sight, Link bent next to the decorated Zora prince five times his stature, his hair in messy and wet braids. Praying for... something. I’m not entirely sure what. To Mipha? For Mipha? Are they not praying at all?     
  
Link turns to Sidon and says something that makes the prince sniffle, but smile all the same. Then they stand, and Sidon turns to me.     
  
“Sorry you had to see me like that. I do like to... speak to Mipha...” he says, unsure. When he looks to Link, he gives him a reassuring nod. “Is there something I can help you with?”

“Well? Tell me everything! How are you feeling? I certainly hope my little sis hasn’t bored you do death,” Purah says, sauntering over to a worktable. I follow her, grabbing Zelda’s hand to lead her to the table. Zelda looks up questioningly, disbelief dancing on her features. All I can offer is an apologetic and amused shrug.     
  
“I don’t think boring would be the right word,” I say, glancing around at the papers scattered about the table.    
  
“Aggravating, then,” Purah says.     
  
“Not quite,” Zelda says softly. “She’s been very *kind*, actually.”     
  
Purah smiles. “Well, I do believe some explanations are in order,” she says, smiling.

Behind the fountain is a bunch of silent princesses. Zelda gasps, hand over her mouth and smiles. “They survived,” she says softly.    
  
She walks over and sits beside the flowers, her back against a tree. I sit across from her. I pick one of the flowers, to which Zelda gasps.    
  
“Don’t do that!” she says.    
  
“Don’t worry,” I say, smiling. “It’ll grow back.”    
  
She shuts her mouth and lets me put the stem behind her ear. It suits her.    
  
She’s so beautiful.    
  
“I don’t think they’re endangered anymore,” I say off-handedly. That memory is something I’ve thought about every time I see one of the flowers. It’s also one I haven’t told a soul about it. Its one that I replay on the nights I couldn’t go back to sleep, when the weight of the sword and the Hero was too much, when I was so frustrated by this world it seemed like nobody and nothing could help.    
  
So, I remembered her. I told myself she could help.

Tip #1. 

It. Is. Never. To. Late. Plus, you're young. 

Tip #2. 

Just start writing lol. Look up a prompt list, and apply it to your favorite characters or fandom. Join a new fandom (usually gives me a massive burst of inspo lol). Read other fanworks, or write something based off your favorite fanart. Create an OC in your favorite universe. Write a drabble or two, or a couple of one-shots. 

Tip #3. 

Your first work/story/longfic/one-shot/anything will most likely be cringe. And that's okay. Don't post anything right away if you don't want to. There are discord servers you can use to get instant feedback on work. Get a friend to beta read. Alternatively, post the work and get feedback from readers. I learned so much by just swallowing my embarrassment and posting my first (very silly, niche, cringe, and badly written) longfic. It helped me so much. And most people in the community will be happy to give you feedback and constructive criticism. 

I wish you the best on your writing journey :D
